statement: From a tree, Rosa walks 3 km north, then 4 km east, then 6 km south, then 8 km west. How far is she now from the tree, in a straight line?

choices.misconception: I added up all four distances she walked instead of finding how far she ended from the tree.
I found she ended 3 km south and 4 km west of the tree, then added those two distances instead of using the straight line.
I added the north and south distances and the east and west distances instead of subtracting opposite directions, then used a right triangle with sides 9 and 12.
I used only the last two legs, 6 and 8, as the sides of a right triangle.

hints: Sketch her path and mark where she ends.
Draw the walk on a grid with the tree at the start. Opposite directions cancel, so find how far south and how far west she ends up, then join her end point straight to the tree.
North 3 then south 6 leaves her 3 km south; east 4 then west 8 leaves her 4 km west. The straight line is the long side of a right triangle with sides 3 and 4.

solutions.reliable: Treat north-south and east-west separately. Going 3 km north and then 6 km south leaves Rosa 3 km south of the tree. Going 4 km east and then 8 km west leaves her 4 km west. Her straight-line distance is the long side of a right triangle with legs 3 and 4, which is 5 km, since 3 x 3 + 4 x 4 = 25 = 5 x 5. The transferable idea: when directions are described in words, draw them; opposite moves cancel and the picture shows the triangle.

whyOnTest: Direction problems are easy once drawn, and the wrong choices come from adding legs that should cancel or skipping the sketch.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
